intro: A new tenant on the third floor, a narrator who watches him, and a building full of talk: the story sorts every statement about the man by its source and by how sure the speaker is. What the neighbours pass on is hearsay (soll); what the man and Frau Albers say about themselves is a claim the narrator keeps at arm's length (will); what the narrator concludes from the evidence — the early mornings, the heavy book boxes, the grey letters with a coat of arms, the fluent Russian — runs down the certainty scale from sure to ruled out. Twelve gaps, each hint giving only the English meaning (people say, he claims, surely, probably, possibly, may well, impossible, hardly likely). Six of the gaps are about the past: the modal stays in the present and the Infinitiv II follows (gelebt haben, gewogen haben, verbracht haben, gewesen sein, gesehen haben, gearbeitet haben). Read to the end first — the final scene with the parcel resolves the tension.
tips[0].title: Who is the source? soll vs will
tips[0].text: soll relays what other people say (the rumours in the building); will relays what the subject says about himself or herself, and signals that the narrator does not vouch for it. Both keep the claim at a distance — the difference is who is speaking.
tips[0].trap: will + Infinitiv II is not "wants to have": Er will … gearbeitet haben = he claims to have worked. And don't double the hearsay: Man sagt, er soll … is redundant — soll already means "people say".
tips[0].check.why: The claim comes from other people, so it is soll. will would mean he claims it himself; muss would be the narrator's own firm conclusion.
tips[0].visual.rows[0].b: Er will nie in Berlin gewesen sein.
tips[1].title: How sure is the narrator? The certainty scale
tips[1].text: muss (a firm conclusion) > dürfte (probably) > könnte / kann (possibly) > mag (conceding: "that may well be so, but …") > kann nicht (ruled out). The narrator's evidence decides the step: a strict routine → muss; an estimate → dürfte; one explanation among others → könnte; a letter that comes every week → kann nicht.
tips[1].trap: dürfte here is not "would be allowed to" but "probably"; könnte is not ability but possibility.
tips[1].check.why: dürfte expresses ‘probably’, an estimate. muss is a firm conclusion, and will / soll report what someone says.
tips[2].title: Past supposition: modal now + Infinitiv II
tips[2].text: The supposition is made now, about then: the modal stays in the present (or the Konjunktiv II for dürfte / könnte), and the past moves into the infinitive — Partizip II + haben / sein at the very end.
tips[2].trap: Not "Er hat im Ausland verbringen können" — that is objective ability (he was able to). The supposition needs the Infinitiv II.
tips[2].check.why: A guess about the past keeps the modal now and puts Partizip II + sein at the end: gewesen sein (sein takes sein).
table.caption: The modals in the story
remember[0]: soll = other people say it; will = the subject says it about himself. Certainty: muss > dürfte > könnte > mag > kann nicht.
remember[1]: Past supposition: modal in the present + Partizip II + haben / sein (soll gelebt haben, dürften gewogen haben).
hook: Who is the mysterious tenant on the third floor? Follow the rumours and learn to say exactly how sure you are.
